title: The knee of the heart
sum: A king in chains prays. The prayer gives itself to Manasseh, the king of Judah who, in Kings, filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, and who, in Chronicles, was led to Babylon in fetters and there humbled himself and prayed (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). It moves in three steps. First it praises God as maker and master of everything, whose anger no one can stand but whose mercy has no measure (1:1–7). Then it turns: repentance was never set for the righteous, but "for me, the sinner" (1:8). The king confesses sins more than the sand of the sea and his body bent by a heavy iron chain (1:9–10). Last he bends "my heart's knee," begs to be let go, and vows to praise God all his days (1:11–15).

The prayer is short and names no event, so it has served for centuries as everyone's prayer of repentance. Its theology fits the Bible: God's mercy is greater than any sin, and repentance is a gift God gives to sinners. Its standing differs from church to church. The Orthodox read it at Great Compline, mostly in Lent; the Clementine Vulgate printed it in an appendix; Anglicans and Lutherans keep it among the books read but not used for doctrine; Reformed churches and Judaism do not count it as Scripture (see the book page).
readings: Taken at its word, the prayer is what the king said in Babylon, the prayer 2 Chronicles 33:18–19 says was written down. Read this way, every line has a place in his life: the idols of 1:10 are those of 2 Chronicles 33:3–7, the iron chain answers to the Assyrian fetters, and the vow of 1:15 is kept when he returns and restores the altar (2 Chronicles 33:16). No church has to settle the question for the prayer to be prayed, and the Orthodox Church reads it without ruling on its author.
Read as a later writer's prayer for Manasseh

Most scholars think a pious Jew of a later age composed the prayer to fill Chronicles' gap, the way speeches and prayers were added to Esther and Daniel in Greek. The Jewish Encyclopedia judged that it "can not be definitively" dated or placed. Read this way, it shows how Jews of the last centuries before Christ thought about the worst sinner of their history: if God heard Manasseh, he would hear anyone.

From the Apostolic Constitutions, which use the story as a lesson for bishops on receiving penitents, to the Orthodox service of Great Compline, Christians have used the prayer to teach and to pray repentance. Read this way, "the sinner" is whoever prays it.

views.O: In the Orthodox Church the prayer is read at Great Compline, the long evening service sung mostly in Lent. In the second part of the service it is the third of three psalms, after Psalm 51 (Psalm 50 in the Greek numbering) and Psalm 102 (101), before the Trisagion prayers; some service books give it to the priest rather than the reader (DiPippo). An Orthodox Church in America parish publishing These Truths We Hold calls it "read at the Great Compline Service" and says the church "accepts these books as being canonical," though not as primary sources for dogma.
views.H: An anonymous composition, set in the gap of 2 Chronicles 33:18–19. Its earliest attested use is in Christian church orders, the Didascalia Apostolorum and the Apostolic Constitutions (Jewish Encyclopedia; Metzger), and in the odes of Codex Alexandrinus in the 400s. Scholars differ on its language (Greek: Porter, Swete; Hebrew: Ewald, Budde; Metzger: disputed) and date it before or around the time of Christ (Metzger: "shortly before the beginning of the Christian Era"; Bowker: the end of the first century BC).
views.J: The prayer is not in the Jewish Bible, and the Jewish Encyclopedia found "no trace" of it in Jewish tradition. But the rabbis argued over Manasseh's repentance. The Mishnah lists him among three kings with no share in the world to come; Rabbi Judah disagreed, and the sages answered that God restored his kingdom, not his share (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). The Jewish Encyclopedia reports a legend in the Jerusalem Talmud that he prayed to his idols in vain from an iron mule over a fire, and was saved when he cried to the God of his fathers.
views.N: The prayer's words about repentance are close to the Gospels': repentance is for sinners, not the righteous (1:8; Luke 5:32; Luke 15:7), "me, the sinner" (1:8; Luke 18:13), the downcast eyes (1:9; Luke 18:13), "I have sinned" (1:12; Luke 15:18). No New Testament book quotes the prayer; these are shared ways of speaking about God's mercy, and they show how a Jew of Jesus' time could pray.
views.W: In the West the prayer was printed but set apart. The Council of Trent's list does not include it, and the Clementine Vulgate placed it after the New Testament, outside "the series of canonical Scripture," with 3 and 4 Esdras. Article VI of the Church of England lists "The Prayer of Manasses" among the books read "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not to establish doctrine. Luther kept it among the Apocrypha (Jewish Encyclopedia). The Westminster Confession says the books called Apocrypha "are no part of the Canon of Scripture."

deep.b:
The prayer has no Hebrew text and stands in no book of the Hebrew Bible. It survives in three kinds of places. (1) In Christian church orders: the Jewish Encyclopedia says it is in the Didascalia, after a mention of 2 Chronicles 33, and in the Apostolic Constitutions (book 2, section 22), which tell the whole story of Manasseh as a lesson for bishops and end it with the chains falling off in a flame of fire. (2) Among the odes or canticles copied after the Psalms in Greek manuscripts, where Codex Alexandrinus has it and Swete prints it as his eighth Ode; Swete's Introduction lists it among the canticles of the Zurich Psalter (600s AD). (3) In Latin manuscripts of the Vulgate, where the Jewish Encyclopedia says it sometimes stands at the end of 2 Chronicles, and Metzger says pre-Trent editions printed it after 2 Chronicles; the Latin is not Jerome's.

English readers knew it from the Apocrypha of the KJV, where it is "The Prayer of Manasses,".

Kings and Chronicles tell Manasseh's reign in almost the same words (2 Kings 21:1–9; 2 Chronicles 33:1–9) and then part ways. In Kings the prophets announce disaster (2 Kings 21:10–15), and later Kings blames the exile on "the sins of Manasseh" (2 Kings 24:3). In Chronicles, God's punishment comes at once, the king humbles himself, God hears, and he is restored and repairs the damage (2 Chronicles 33:10–16). This prayer belongs to the Chronicles ending. It does not deny Kings: Chronicles still says his sin and unfaithfulness were written down (2 Chronicles 33:19). It shows the worst king of Judah forgiven, the strongest case a Bible reader could make that no sinner is beyond God's mercy.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a prayer built from Chronicles' own words
deep.b: Two words in 2 Chronicles 33:12–13 may have shaped the prayer. Chronicles says Manasseh "humbled himself deeply" and that God "was entreated by him" and "heard his pleading." The prayer is made of exactly those two acts: humbling (the bent body, the bent knee of the heart, 1:10–11) and entreaty ("I ask you, I beg you," 1:13). And the frame of verses 1–7, praise of the God who rules the heavens, fits a king whose sin was worshiping "the army of the heavens" (2 Chronicles 33:3; 2 Chronicles 33:5), the point of the note at 1:15. If so, the author did not invent a prayer at random but wrote the one Chronicles implies. This is Claude's suggestion; no source opened for this page makes the argument.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 33:10–19; 2 Kings 21:1–18; Exodus 34:6–7; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 51:1–17; Genesis 22:17; Luke 5:32; Luke 15:7; Luke 15:18; Luke 18:13; Daniel 9:4–19

settings.by: Manasseh king of Judah, as the heading presents him
settings.when: as 1:10 and 2 Chronicles 33:11 suggest, in captivity in Babylon, where 2 Chronicles 33:11–13 says he humbled himself and prayed
settings.why: To be heard and set free: the king praises God's power and mercy, confesses that his sins are past counting, and asks to be let go and spared from death. In Chronicles the answer is that God "heard his pleading and brought him back."
settings.readers: Unknown by name. Most likely Jews, before or around the time of Christ, who read Chronicles and wanted the words of the prayer it mentions; then Christians, whose church orders (the Didascalia and the Apostolic Constitutions) used it to teach bishops to receive the repentant, and who later prayed it in worship. On Nestle's view the first readers were Christian clergy.
views: The Jewish Encyclopedia judged the author "evidently a Jew," and Metzger dated the prayer "shortly before the beginning of the Christian Era" and found its thought closer to Palestinian than to Greek-speaking Judaism; Bowker puts it at the end of the first century BC.

Its oldest known copies are in Christian church orders and Christian manuscripts. The Jewish Encyclopedia reports Eberhard Nestle's view that the text of the Greek manuscripts came from the Didascalia or the Constitutions; on this view the prayer's first known readers were Christian clergy learning how to treat penitents. The introduction in Charles's Apocrypha judges instead that the prayer was most probably written in Greek, before the church orders quoted it.
